what: Silicon Motion designs the controller chips that manage NAND flash memory inside solid-state drives, smartphones, memory cards and industrial devices. It is the largest independent supplier of these controllers, selling to flash makers and module makers who do not design their own. Its American depositary shares each represent four ordinary shares.
customers: NAND flash manufacturers and module makers, PC and smartphone brands, and industrial and automotive customers through its Ferri product line.
money: Controllers for client and enterprise solid-state drives.
Embedded storage controllers for smartphones, tablets and consumer devices.
Ferri embedded storage for industrial and automotive use, and SD card controllers.
moat: Controller design requires deep firmware expertise for each generation of NAND, and flash makers that do not build their own controllers rely on a handful of independent suppliers. Silicon Motion’s long relationships with those makers and its range across PCs, phones and industrial uses give it scale that smaller rivals lack, though the largest memory makers can always bring the work in-house.
risks: Revenue follows the boom-and-bust cycle of NAND flash, falling 32% in 2023 before recovering.
Operating cash flow turned negative at minus $350M over the last twelve months as inventory and receivables ballooned during the memory upturn.
Large memory makers such as Samsung design their own controllers and could take more work in-house.
The company is based in Taiwan and sells heavily into China, which adds geopolitical and export-control risk.
The abandoned MaxLinear merger in 2023 left a legal dispute and showed how dependent the business is on outside events.
opportunities: Revenue over the last twelve months almost doubled to $1.63B, and net income rose to $316M, as AI-driven demand lifted the whole memory market.
Forward earnings put the shares on under 7 times, if the upturn holds.
Enterprise SSD controllers for AI data centres are a newer, higher-value market where Silicon Motion is gaining customers.
The company pays a dividend of about 1.7% and holds $846M of cash.
watch: NAND pricing and inventory, the conversion of working capital back into cash, enterprise SSD design wins, and any reversal in memory demand.
view: Silicon Motion is a cyclical stock wearing a value costume. A forward price-to-earnings ratio under 7 looks absurdly cheap, but that number assumes the current memory boom continues; in a NAND upcycle, revenue and earnings rise faster than anyone models, and in the downturn they fall just as fast. Revenue fell from $946M in 2022 to $639M in 2023 before the AI-driven recovery took it to $1.63B over the last twelve months.

The number that worries me is cash. Net income over the last twelve months was $316M, but operating cash flow was minus $350M, and debt has risen to $1.13B. That is what happens when a fabless chip company builds inventory and extends credit to customers in a shortage. It can be perfectly rational, but it means the earnings have not yet been turned into money, and if the cycle turns while the warehouse is full, the write-downs follow.

The investment turns on whether this upturn is longer than usual because of AI storage demand. Enterprise SSDs for data centres are a genuine new market, and Silicon Motion’s wins there would support a higher floor in the next downturn. Still, I would not treat the low forward P/E as a margin of safety. This is a cycle trade: attractive early, dangerous late, and the cash flow statement suggests we are not early.
bull: AI storage demand keeps NAND tight through 2027, working capital turns back into cash and enterprise controllers lift through-cycle earnings.
bear: The memory cycle turns, inventory has to be written down and earnings collapse as they did in 2023.
